module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 307

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/307](https://www.erdosproblems.com/307)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos307

open scoped Finset

/--
Are there two finite set of primes $P$ and $Q$ such that

$$
1 = \left( \sum_{p \in P} \frac{1}{p} \right) \left( \sum_{q \in Q} \frac{1}{q} \right)
$$
?

Asked by Barbeau [Ba76].

[Ba76] Barbeau, E. J., _Computer challenge corner: Problem 477: A brute force program._
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_307 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, (∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
Instead of asking for sets of primes, ask only that all elements in the sets be relatively coprime.

Cambie has found several examples when this weakened version is true. For example,
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{5}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}\right)
$$
and
$$
1=\left(1+\frac{1}{41}\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{7}\right).
$$
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime : answer(True) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧
    Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  show True ↔ _
  simp only [Finset.mem_inter, not_and, true_iff]
  use {1, 5}, {2, 3}
  norm_num +decide

/--
There are no examples known of the weakened coprime version if we insist that $1\not\in P\cup Q$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_307.variants.coprime_one_notMem : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ P Q : Finset ℕ, 0 ∉ P ∩ Q ∧ 1 ∉ P ∪ Q ∧
    1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ Set.Pairwise P Nat.Coprime ∧ Set.Pairwise Q Nat.Coprime ∧
    1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹) := by
  sorry

/--
A machine-checked **barrier** for Erdős 307 (Bonfioli, 2026): any solution with `Q` nonempty uses at
least 59 primes in total, and `(∏_{p ∈ P} p)² ≥ 4·10¹¹²` — i.e. `∏_{p ∈ P} p ≥ 2·10⁵⁶` (and, by
symmetry, the same for `∏ Q`); so no solution lies below a prime-product of `2.09·10⁵⁶`. The full
`sorry`-free proof is in the linked repository (`Closed.lean`): the left conjunct is `card_ge_59`,
the right is `erdos307_barrier_closed`. Both depend on `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` and
nothing further: the evaluation of the first 59 primes is kernel-checked by `decide`, so no
`native_decide` enters this statement.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/76d242b024102f32d8411c714be4ad140a8b7c4b/lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean#L121"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime) (hQne : Q.Nonempty)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    59 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) ∧ (4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2 := by
  sorry

/--
A stronger machine-checked **barrier** (Bonfioli, 2026), closing the 59-prime level: any solution of
Erdős 307 in fact uses at least `60` primes in total. The full `sorry`-free proof is `erdos307_sixty`
in the linked repository (`Sixty.lean` at tag `v1.1.1`); its only non-logical input is a `native_decide`
depth-first search establishing that no admissible 59-prime support survives the Pythagorean
`plus`-value square test, with axioms `propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound` together with that
`native_decide`.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11, formal_proof using lean4 at
"https://github.com/ElVec1o/erdos307/blob/080164a8db2eeb20f65c362894ec93f12448609a/lean/Erdos307/Sixty.lean#L367"]
theorem erdos_307.barrier_sixty {P Q : Finset ℕ}
    (hP : ∀ p ∈ P, p.Prime) (hQ : ∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime)
    (heq : 1 = (∑ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)⁻¹) * (∑ q ∈ Q, (q : ℚ)⁻¹)) :
    60 ≤ #(P ∪ Q) := by
  sorry

end Erdos307

findings.description: The docstring correctly says the conclusion `(4 * 10 ^ 112 : ℚ) ≤ (∏ p ∈ P, (p : ℚ)) ^ 2` means ∏P ≥ 2·10⁵⁶ (and, by symmetry, the same for ∏Q). It then adds "so no solution lies below a prime-product of 2.09·10⁵⁶". That does not follow: 2·10⁵⁶ < 2.09·10⁵⁶. The constant 2.09·10⁵⁶ is the sharp value from the paper, which is not formalized. The Lean statement itself is correct: I checked that the linked proof establishes it.
findings.source_evidence: The linked file (ElVec1o/erdos307 @76d242b, lean/Erdos307/Closed.lean, header) says: "Note the constant. The paper's `thm:barrier` states the sharp `2.09·10⁵⁶`; what is machine-checked here is the rounded `2·10⁵⁶`, which is what the explicit rational core `barrier_numeric` carries. The sharp value is a paper result, not a Lean one." The README of the same repository gives the paper's result as `min(∏P, ∏Q) ≥ 2.09 × 10⁵⁶`.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the last clause with: "so min(∏P, ∏Q) ≥ 2·10⁵⁶ for any solution (the paper's sharp constant 2.09·10⁵⁶ is not part of this statement)".

reformulations.difference: The source asks whether the weakened version (each of P and Q made of relatively coprime integers) has an example with 1 ∉ P ∪ Q. The Lean adds the side conditions `0 ∉ P ∩ Q`, `1 < #P` and `1 < #Q`. It also imposes pairwise coprimality within P and within Q separately, not across all of P ∪ Q.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: (1) The side conditions are redundant. If 0 ∈ P, pairwise coprimality forces every other element to be 1 (`Nat.coprime_zero_left`). Since 1 ∉ P and #P ≥ 2, this is impossible, so every element is ≥ 2. Conversely, for pairwise coprime elements ≥ 2 the fraction ∑1/a = N/∏a is in lowest terms: a prime dividing a member divides every cofactor ∏_{b≠x} b except one. So a nonempty such family never has an integer reciprocal sum. Hence #P = 1 (σ(Q) = a ∈ ℕ) and #P = 0 (product 0) are both impossible, and likewise for Q. (2) Coprimality within each set plus the equation forces coprimality across the sets. Clearing denominators gives N_P·N_Q = D_P·D_Q. A prime dividing some p ∈ P and some q ∈ Q would divide D_P·D_Q but neither N_P nor N_Q. So the source's literal reading ("relatively coprime, and similarly for Q") and the reading "all of P ∪ Q pairwise coprime" coincide with the Lean. A setwise-gcd reading is excluded by the source, because it has the trivial example P={2,3}, Q={2,3,5,6} (checked in Lean), which contradicts the page's "no examples known". Proved in scratch: `Review.rhs_equiv` shows the Lean RHS ↔ ∃ P Q, (∀ x ∈ P ∪ Q, 2 ≤ x) ∧ pairwise coprime within each ∧ equation. `Review.cross_coprime` shows the equation plus coprimality within each set implies ∀ p ∈ P, ∀ q ∈ Q, Coprime p q. Both use only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].

reformulations.difference: The Lean does not require P and Q to be nonempty or disjoint. The MathOverflow form of the problem (MO 320838) asks for solutions in distinct primes p_1..p_k, q_1..q_l.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An empty set gives sum 0, so the product is 0 ≠ 1. A prime in P ∩ Q contradicts the forced cross-coprimality: sets of distinct primes are pairwise coprime, so `cross_coprime` applies, and a prime is not coprime to itself. Proved in scratch as `Review.main_equiv`, using only [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]. The page itself remarks that P and Q must be disjoint.

review.notes:
I found no misformalization. Per declaration:

- `erdos_307` states the page's question verbatim ("Are there two finite sets of primes P, Q such that 1 = (∑1/p)(∑1/q)?"). It is `research open` with `answer(sorry)`, which matches the page status VERIFIABLE (open). Degenerate witnesses are impossible: empty sets give product 0, and P = Q or overlapping sets are ruled out (proved).
- `variants.coprime` is proved with Cambie's example {1,5},{2,3}, using only the standard axioms. The side conditions `1 < #P ∧ 1 < #Q ∧ 0 ∉ P ∩ Q` exclude the trivial witnesses {1},{1} and {0,1},{0,1}. `answer(True)` matches "Cambie has found several examples". The `textbook` category is defensible.
- `variants.coprime_one_notMem` is equivalent to the source question (proved; see reformulations).

Pairwise coprimality within each set is the only reading of "relatively coprime" that fits the page's "no examples known" when 1 ∉ P∪Q. Under a setwise-gcd reading, (1/2+1/3)(1/2+1/3+1/5+1/6) = 1 (machine-checked). Cambie's forum comment also says the cross-only and setwise versions have positive answers.

**`formal_proof` claims.** I compiled both linked developments at their pinned commits in the sandbox (Lean v4.33.1; they target v4.30.0, but only deprecation warnings appeared).
- I proved `type_of% @Erdos307.erdos_307.barrier` from `card_ge_59` and `erdos307_barrier_closed`. The axioms are only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, as the docstring says.
- I proved `type_of% @Erdos307.erdos_307.barrier_sixty` from `erdos307_sixty`. It needs no `sorry`.

Both records are valid, and I found no status issue.

**Proof-provenance nit (not mathematical).** The `barrier_sixty` docstring says its "only non-logical input is a native_decide depth-first search". At commit 080164a (= tag v1.1.1), `#print axioms erdos307_sixty` lists 69 `_native.native_decide` auxiliary axioms. Besides `dfs_run`, these include the Numeral bridge np0–np58 (`Nat.count Nat.Prime` facts) and the forced39/pool99 facts. The newest upstream (v1.75.0) says it no longer uses `native_decide` anywhere, so the link could be refreshed.

**The page's "whence |P∪Q| ≥ 60" remark.** The easy argument only gives 59. I checked with `#eval` that the reciprocal sum of the first 58 primes is 1.99874 < 2 < 2.00235 for the first 59 (the 59th prime is 277). The bound 60 needs Bonfioli's computation, and the file correctly states it separately as `barrier_sixty`. I also checked that 4·10¹¹²·σ₅₉ ≤ Π₅₉, where Π₅₉/σ₅₉ ≈ 4.38·10¹¹².

**Primary literature I could not reach.** The Erdős–Graham 1980 PDF (p. 38) is an image scan on an unreachable host, and I could not access Barbeau 1976 (J. Rec. Math.). This did not affect any verdict, because the cited page and MathOverflow agree on the statement.
